content: Citrus canker is a bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis that affects various citrus species, including lime, oranges, and grapefruit. The infection results in the formation of lesions on the leaves, stems, and fruit of citrus trees. While the disease does not pose any risk to human health, it significantly impacts the health of citrus trees, leading to premature leaf and fruit drop. Although the fruit remains safe for consumption, its appearance becomes unsuitable for commercial sale. The disease is believed to have originated in Southeast Asia and is notoriously difficult to eradicate once established in an area. Complete destruction of all citrus orchards in the affected region is often required to eliminate the disease. Currently, countries such as Australia, Brazil, and the United States are experiencing outbreaks of citrus canker. The causative agent, Xanthomonas axonopodis, is a rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacterium equipped with polar flagella. Its genome is approximately 5 megabase pairs in length. Several types of citrus canker exist, each caused by different pathovars or variants of the bacterium. The most severe and widespread form, Asiatic canker (Canker A), is caused by X. axonopodis pv. citri and was originally identified in Asia. Cancrosis B, caused by X. axonopodis pv. aurantifolii, primarily affects lemons, key lime, bitter orange, and pomelo and is native to South America. Cancrosis C, also caused by X. axonopodis pv. aurantifolii, is limited to infecting key lime and bitter orange. Another variant, known as A-strains, has been identified in regions such as Oman, Saudi Arabia, Iran, and India, and it exclusively infects key lime. Plants infected with citrus canker exhibit distinctive lesions on their leaves, stems, and fruit. These lesions are raised, brown, and water-soaked, often surrounded by a yellow halo. Over time, older lesions develop a corky texture but may still retain the halo effect. The bacterium multiplies within these lesions, and bacterial cells can ooze out, spreading to other plants via wind and rain. Severe weather events, such as hurricanes and tornadoes, can exacerbate the spread of the disease. Additionally, human activities, such as the use of contaminated equipment, contact with infected trees, and the transport of infected plants or fruit, can facilitate the transmission of the bacterium. The bacteria enter plants through natural openings like stomata or through wounds on leaves and other green tissues. Young leaves are particularly vulnerable to infection, and damage caused by the larvae of the citrus leaf miner (Phyllocnistis citrella) can create entry points for the bacteria. Symptoms of the disease typically appear 14 to 60 days or more after infection. The bacteria can remain viable in old lesions and on plant surfaces for several months. Citrus canker can be identified in orchards and on fruit by the characteristic appearance of lesions. Early detection is crucial, especially in quarantine situations. Pathogenicity tests are conducted by inoculating various citrus species with the bacterium, and additional diagnostic methods, such as antibody detection, fatty acid profiling, and genetic analysis using PCR, are employed to confirm the specific strain of the bacterium. Most citrus varieties are susceptible to citrus canker, although some species exhibit greater resistance than others. In countries where the disease is not present, strict quarantine protocols are implemented to prevent its introduction. In regions with new outbreaks, eradication programs are initiated promptly and often involve the destruction of affected orchards. In areas where eradication is not feasible, management strategies include replacing susceptible citrus cultivars with resistant ones, applying copper-based bactericides as preventive sprays, and removing infected trees along with surrounding trees within a defined radius. Citrus canker is believed to have originated in the Southeast Asia-India region. It has since spread to Japan, South and Central Africa, the Middle East, the Pacific Islands, parts of South America, and Florida. While some regions have successfully eradicated the disease, it remains endemic in many areas where it has been introduced. The disease poses a significant threat to citrus-growing regions due to its rapid spread, potential for severe damage, and negative impact on both domestic trade and export markets. In Australia, the citrus industry is the largest exporter of fresh fruit. The country has experienced three outbreaks of citrus canker, two of which were successfully eradicated. The first outbreak occurred in 1912 in the Northern Territory, leading to the destruction of all citrus trees north of latitude 19° South, a process that took 11 years. In 2004, Asiatic citrus canker was detected in Emerald, Queensland, likely due to the illegal importation of infected citrus plants. In response, state and federal authorities mandated the destruction of all commercial and non-commercial citrus trees, as well as native lime trees (C. glauca) in the affected area. In Brazil, citrus is a vital crop for both domestic consumption and export. The state of São Paulo, the world’s largest producer of sweet oranges, has over 100,000 orchards, with more than 80% of the trees being a single orange variety. This lack of genetic diversity has made the region particularly vulnerable to citrus canker, resulting in significant crop and financial losses. In Brazil, management efforts focus on destroying infected trees and those within a 30-meter radius, rather than entire orchards. By 1998, over half a million trees had been destroyed. In the United States, citrus canker was first identified in 1910 near the Georgia-Florida border. The disease spread rapidly, reaching Dade County, Florida, within two years. By 1931, after a 20-year eradication effort costing $2.5 million (equivalent to $28 million in 2000), the outbreak was successfully controlled. However, the disease reappeared in Florida in 1986 and was eradicated again. The most recent outbreak began in 1995 near Miami International Airport. Despite eradication efforts, the disease spread across much of Florida by 2005, likely facilitated by hurricanes in 2004 and 2005. The spread following Hurricane Wilma in October 2005 significantly reduced citrus production estimates. A USDA study projected that over 183,000 acres (741 km²) of citrus groves, representing 25% of the total citrus area, could be destroyed due to the outbreak. Active eradication programs and sentinel tree surveys continue in Florida to monitor and control the disease.
